claims.text: Grain-boundary engineering can improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss in high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary engineering promotes formation of ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layers in high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary engineering reduces the energy of high-angle grain boundaries.
The proposed intervention applies to high-entropy alloys in an as-cast or as-fabricated initial state.
Surface mechanical attrition treatment is an example of the proposed grain-boundary-engineering intervention.
Cryogenic thermal cycling is an example of the proposed grain-boundary-engineering intervention.
The hypothesis is intended to hold after exposure at approximately 500°C for approximately 100 hours.
Ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layers are a structural mediator of the proposed improvement in thermal-toughness retention.
High-angle grain boundaries are a structural mediator of the proposed improvement in thermal-toughness retention.
Formation of ultra-nanocrystalline surface layers and reduction of high-angle grain-boundary energy improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss.
Treated alloys will exhibit a smaller decrease in Charpy impact energy after high-temperature exposure than untreated alloys.
The baseline is an otherwise comparable high-entropy alloy without grain-boundary engineering.
The improvement should be greatest in alloys having a high initial fraction of high-angle grain boundaries.
The improvement should be greatest in alloys having low initial toughness.
The magnitude of improvement depends on alloy composition, treatment, and test conditions.
